passage_1.text:
The Positivists, anxious to stake out their claim for history as a science, contributed the weight of their influence to the cult of facts. First ascertain the facts, said the positivists, then draw your conclusions from them. This is what may be called the common-sense view of history. History consists of a corpus of ascertained facts. The facts are available to the historian in documents, inscriptions, and so on. Sir George Clark contrasted the "hard core of facts" in history with the surrounding pulp of disputable interpretation forgetting perhaps that the pulpy part of the fruit is more rewarding than the hard core. It recalls the favourite dictum of the great liberal journalist C. P. Scott: "Facts are sacred, opinion is free."

What is a historical fact? According to the common-sense view, there are certain basic facts which are the same for all historians and which form, so to speak, the backbone of history-the fact, for example, that the Battle of Hastings was fought in 1066. But this view calls for two observations. In the first place, it is not with facts like these that the historian is primarily concerned. It is no doubt important to know that the great battle was fought in 1066 and not in 1065 or 1067, and that it was fought at Hastings and not at Eastbourne or Brighton. The historian must not get these things wrong. But to praise a historian for his accuracy is like praising an architect for using well-seasoned timber or properly mixed concrete in his building. It is a necessary condition of his work, but not his essential function. It is precisely for matters of this kind that the historian is entitled to rely on what have been called the "auxiliary sciences" of history—archaeology, epigraphy, numismatics, chronology, and so forth.

The second observation is that the necessity to establish these basic facts rests not on any quality in the facts themselves, but on an apriori decision of the historian. In spite of C. P. Scott's motto, every journalist knows today that the most effective way to influence opinion is by the selection and arrangement of the appropriate facts. It used to be said that facts speak for themselves. This is, of course, untrue. The facts speak only when the historian calls on them: it is he who decides to which facts to give the floor, and in what order or context. The only reason why we are interested to know that the battle was fought at Hastings in 1066 is that historians regard it as a major historical event. Professor Talcott Parsons once called science "a selective system of cognitive orientations to reality." It might perhaps have been put more simply. But history is, among other things, that. The historian is necessarily selective. The belief in a hard core of historical facts existing objectively and independently of the interpretation of the historian is a preposterous fallacy, but one which it is very hard to eradicate.

passage_2.text:
Over the past four centuries liberalism has been so successful that it has driven all its opponents off the battlefield. Now it is disintegrating, destroyed by a mix of hubris and internal contradictions, according to Patrick Deneen, a professor of politics at the University of Notre Dame. Equality of opportunity has produced a new meritocratic aristocracy that has all the aloofness of the old aristocracy with none of its sense of noblesse oblige. Democracy has degenerated into a theatre of the absurd. And technological advances are reducing ever more areas of work into meaningless drudgery. "The gap between liberalism's claims about itself and the lived reality of the citizenry" is now so wide that "the lie can no longer be accepted," Mr Deneen writes. What better proof of this than the vision of 1,000 private planes whisking their occupants to Davos to discuss the question of "creating a shared future in a fragmented world"?

Deneen does an impressive job of capturing the current mood of disillusionment, echoing left- wing complaints about rampant commercialism, right-wing complaints about narcissistic and bullying students, and general worries about atomisation and selfishness. But when he concludes that all this adds up to a failure of liberalism, is his argument convincing? He argues that the essence of liberalism lies in freeing individuals from constraints. In fact, liberalism contains a wide range of intellectual traditions which provide different answers to the question of how to trade off the relative claims of rights and responsibilities, individual expression and social ties. Liberals experimented with a range of ideas from devolving power from the centre to creating national education systems.

Mr Deneen's fixation on the essence of liberalism leads to the second big problem of his book: his failure to recognise liberalism's ability to reform itself and address its internal problems. The late 19th century saw America suffering from many of the problems that are reappearing today, including the creation of a business aristocracy, the rise of vast companies, the corruption of politics and the sense that society was dividing into winners and losers. But a wide variety of reformers, working within the liberal tradition, tackled these problems head on. Theodore Roosevelt took on the trusts. Progressives cleaned up government corruption. University reformers modernised academic syllabuses and built ladders of opportunity. Rather than dying, liberalism reformed itself.

Mr Deneen is right to point out that the record of liberalism in recent years has been dismal. He is also right to assert that the world has much to learn from the premodern notions of liberty as self-mastery and self-denial. The biggest enemy of liberalism is not so much atomisation but old-fashioned greed, as members of the Davos elite pile their plates ever higher with perks and share options. But he is wrong to argue that the only way for people to liberate themselves from the contradictions of liberalism is "liberation from liberalism itself". The best way to read "Why Liberalism Failed" is not as a funeral oration but as a call to action: up your game, or else.

passage_3.text:
The Second Hand September campaign, led by Oxfam seeks to encourage shopping at local organisations and charities as alternatives to fast fashion brands such as Primark and Boohoo in the name of saving our planet. As innocent as mindless scrolling through online shops may seem, such consumers are unintentionally or perhaps even knowingly contributing to an industry that uses more energy than aviation.

Brits buy more garments than any other country in Europe, so it comes as no shock that many of those clothes end up in UK landfills each year: 300,000 tonnes of them, to be exact. This waste of clothing is destructive to our planet, releasing greenhouse gasses as clothes are burnt as well as bleeding toxins and dyes into the surrounding soil and water. As ecologist Chelsea Rochman bluntly put it, "The mismanagement of our waste has even come back to haunt us on our dinner plate."

It's not surprising, then, that people are scrambling for a solution, the most common of which is second-hand shopping. Retailers selling consigned clothing are currently expanding at a rapid rate. If everyone bought just one used item in a year, it would save 449 million lbs of waste, equivalent to the weight of 1 million Polar bears. "Thrifting" has increasingly become a trendy practice. London is home to many second-hand, or more commonly coined 'vintage', shops across the city from Bayswater to Brixton.

So you're cool and you care about the planet; you've killed two birds with one stone. But do people simply purchase a second-hand item, flash it on Instagram with #vintage and call it a day without considering whether what they are doing is actually effective?

According to a study commissioned by Patagonia, for instance, older clothes shed more microfibres. These can end up in our rivers and seas after just one wash due to the worn material, thus contributing to microfibre pollution. To break it down, the amount of microfibres released by laundering 100,000 fleece jackets is equivalent to as many as 11,900 plastic grocery bags, and up to 40 per cent of that ends up in our oceans. So where does this leave second-hand consumers? They would be well advised to buy high-quality items that shed less and last longer as this combats both microfibre pollution and excess garments ending up in landfills.

Luxury brands would rather not circulate their latest season stock around the globe to be sold at a cheaper price, which is why companies like ThredUP, a US fashion resale marketplace, have not yet caught on in the UK. There will always be a market for consignment but there is also a whole generation of people who have been taught that only buying new products is the norm; second-hand luxury goods are not in their psyche. Ben Whitaker, director at Liquidation Firm B-Stock, told Prospect that unless recycling becomes cost-effective and filters into mass production, with the right technology to partner it, "high-end retailers would rather put brand before sustainability."

passage_6.text:
Umberto Eco, an Italian writer, was right when he said the language of Europe is translation. Netflix and other deep-pocketed global firms speak it well. Just as the EU employs a small army of translators and interpreters to turn intricate laws or impassioned speeches of Romanian MEPs into the EU's 24 official languages, so do the likes of Netflix. It now offers dubbing in 34 languages and subtitling in a few more.

The economics of European productions are more appealing, too. American audiences are more willing than before to give dubbed or subtitled viewing a chance. This means shows such as "Lupin", a French crime caper on Netflix, can become global hits. In 2015, about 75% of Netflix's original content was American; now the figure is half, according to Ampere, a media- analysis company. Netflix has about 100 productions under way in Europe, which is more than big public broadcasters in France or Germany.

Not everything works across borders. Comedy sometimes struggles. Whodunits and bloodthirsty maelstroms between arch Romans and uppity tribesmen have a more universal appeal. Some do it better than others. Barbarians aside, German television is not always built for export, says one executive, being polite. A bigger problem is that national broadcasters still dominate. Streaming services, such as Netflix or Disney+, account for about a third of all viewing hours, even in markets where they are well-established. Europe is an ageing continent. The generation of teens staring at phones is outnumbered by their elders who prefer to gawp at the box.

In Brussels and national capitals, the prospect of Netflix as a cultural hegemon is seen as a threat. "Cultural sovereignty" is the watchword of European executives worried that the Americans will eat their lunch. To be fair, Netflix content sometimes seems stuck in an uncanny valley somewhere in the mid-Atlantic, with local quirks stripped out. Netflix originals tend to have fewer specific cultural references than shows produced by domestic rivals, according to Enders, a market analyst. The company used to have an imperial model of commissioning, with executives in Los Angeles cooking up ideas French people might like. Now Netflix has offices across Europe. But ultimately the big decisions rest with American executives. This makes European politicians nervous.

They should not be. An irony of European integration is that it is often American companies that facilitate it. Google Translate makes European newspapers comprehensible, even if a little clunky, for the continent's non-polyglots. American social-media companies make it easier for Europeans to talk politics across borders. (That they do not always like to hear what they say about each other is another matter.) Now Netflix and friends pump the same content into homes across a continent, making culture a cross-border endeavour, too. If Europeans are to share a currency, bail each other out in times of financial need and share vaccines in a pandemic, then they need to have something in common-even if it is just bingeing on the same series. Watching fictitious northern and southern Europeans tear each other apart 2,000 years ago beats doing so in reality.

questions.question_text: According to this passage, which one of the following statements best describes the significance of archaeology for historians?

options.label: A
options.text: Archaeology helps historians to interpret historical facts.

options.label: B
options.text: Archaeology helps historians to ascertain factual accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: Archaeology helps historians to carry out their primary duty.

options.label: D
options.text: Archaeology helps historians to locate the oldest civilisations in history

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the passage says about archaeology's role for historians.

From passage: "It is precisely for matters of this kind that the historian is entitled to rely on what have been called the 'auxiliary sciences' of history—archaeology, epigraphy, numismatics, chronology, and so forth."

The passage talks about basic facts like "the Battle of Hastings was fought in 1066" -> These are factual details that need to be correct -> The author says historians rely on auxiliary sciences (including archaeology) for these basic facts -> But he compares this to an architect using good timber - necessary but not the main job.

So archaeology helps with getting facts right, not with the main work of interpretation.

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> says archaeology helps interpret facts, but passage shows it only helps establish basic facts before interpretation

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> matches exactly what passage says - archaeology helps get basic factual details right (like dates, locations)

🟠 Option 3 -> degree-error -> says archaeology helps with primary duty, but passage clearly states factual accuracy is not the historian's essential function

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> mentions "oldest civilizations" which isn't discussed anywhere in the passage

The key insight: The passage separates getting facts right (what archaeology helps with) from doing history (the historian's main job of selection and interpretation).

questions.question_text: All of the following, if true, can weaken the passage's claim that facts do not speak for themselves, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the truth value of a fact is independent of the historian who expresses it.

options.label: B
options.text: facts, like truth, can be relative: what is fact for person X may not be so for person Y.

options.label: C
options.text: a fact, by its very nature, is objective and universal, irrespective of the context in which it is placed.

options.label: D
options.text: the order in which a series of facts is presented does not have any bearing on the production of meaning.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which option does NOT weaken the passage's main claim that "facts do not speak for themselves."

The passage argues that historians are the ones who select, arrange, and give meaning to facts. Facts need human interpretation - they don't have meaning on their own.

From passage: "The facts speak only when the historian calls on them: it is he who decides to which facts to give the floor, and in what order or context."

From passage: "every journalist knows today that the most effective way to influence opinion is by the selection and arrangement of the appropriate facts."

So the passage says -> facts need historians to interpret them -> historians choose which facts to use and how to present them -> this gives facts their meaning.

The question asks for the option that does NOT weaken this claim. In other words, we need the option that supports or agrees with the passage.

🔴 Option 1 -> weakens passage -> says facts have truth independent of historians, but passage says historians give facts meaning

🟢 Option 2 -> supports passage -> says facts can be relative to different people, which matches the passage's idea that historians interpret facts differently

🔴 Option 3 -> weakens passage -> says facts are objective and universal, but passage says historians must select and interpret them

🔴 Option 4 -> weakens passage -> says order doesn't matter for meaning, but passage specifically mentions "selection and arrangement" as ways to influence opinion

Option 2 is the only one that agrees with the passage's view that facts are not absolute and require human interpretation. All other options contradict the passage by suggesting facts have objective, independent meaning.

questions.question_text: If the author of the passage were to write a book on the Battle of Hastings along the lines of his/her own reasoning, the focus of the historical account would be on:

options.label: A
options.text: providing a nuanced interpretation by relying on the auxiliary sciences.

options.label: B
options.text: producing a detailed timeline of the various events that led to the Battle.

options.label: C
options.text: exploring the socio-political and economic factors that led to the Battle.

options.label: D
options.text: deriving historical facts from the relevant documents and inscriptions.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to understand what the author thinks historians should actually focus on, not what they currently do wrong.

From passage: "It is precisely for matters of this kind that the historian is entitled to rely on what have been called the 'auxiliary sciences' of history... It is a necessary condition of his work, but not his essential function."

The author criticizes historians who just collect basic facts -> says that's like praising an architect for using good concrete -> it's necessary but not the main job -> the real work is interpretation and selection -> deciding which facts matter and why.

From passage: "The facts speak only when the historian calls on them: it is he who decides to which facts to give the floor, and in what order or context."

So the author believes historians should be selective interpreters, not fact-collectors -> they should focus on why events matter and what they mean in context.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> mentions auxiliary sciences, but author says these are just for basic facts, not the main focus of real historical work

🔴 Option 2 -> misses-the-point -> detailed timeline is just more fact-gathering, which author criticizes as not being the historian's essential function

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> explores deeper causes and context, which aligns with author's view that historians should interpret and select meaningful aspects, not just collect basic facts

🔴 Option 4 -> directly-opposite -> deriving facts from documents is exactly what author calls "necessary but not essential" - this is the positivist approach he criticizes

The author would focus on why the battle mattered historically and what forces shaped it, not just when and where it happened.

questions.question_text: All of the following describe the "common-sense view" of history, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: history can be objective like the sciences if it is derived from historical facts.

options.label: B
options.text: real history can be found in ancient engravings and archival documents.

options.label: C
options.text: history is like science: a selective system of cognitive orientations to reality.

options.label: D
options.text: only the positivist methods can lead to credible historical knowledge.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the common-sense view includes, then spot the option that doesn't fit.

The passage clearly outlines the common-sense view: facts first, then conclusions. History = collection of established facts from documents and inscriptions. Facts exist objectively, independent of historian's interpretation.

From passage: "First ascertain the facts, said the positivists, then draw your conclusions from them. This is what may be called the common-sense view of history."

From passage: "The belief in a hard core of historical facts existing objectively and independently of the interpretation of the historian is a preposterous fallacy"

The author calls this view a "fallacy" -> so he disagrees with common-sense view -> author has his own different view.

🟠 Option 1 -> fits common-sense view -> says history can be objective like science through facts (exactly what positivists wanted)

🟠 Option 2 -> fits common-sense view -> mentions documents/inscriptions as source of "real history" (passage says facts available in "documents, inscriptions, and so on")

🟢 Option 3 -> author's view, not common-sense view -> "selective system" quote comes from author criticizing common-sense view. Author says historian is "necessarily selective" - opposite of common-sense belief in objective facts

🟠 Option 4 -> fits common-sense view -> positivists wanted history as science, this supports only their methods

Key confusion: Students might think Option 3 sounds scientific, so it must be common-sense view. But the "selective" part is the author's criticism of common-sense view. Common-sense view believes facts are objective and universal, not selective.

Author's view -> history is selective

Common-sense view -> history is objective facts

Option 3 describes what the author thinks, not what common-sense believers think.

questions.question_text: The author of the passage faults Deneen's conclusions for all of the following reasons, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: its failure to note historical instances in which the process of declining liberalism has managed to reverse itself.

options.label: B
options.text: its extreme pessimism about the future of liberalism today and predictions of an ultimate decline.

options.label: C
options.text: its repeated harking back to premodern notions of liberty.

options.label: D
options.text: its very narrow definition of liberalism limited to individual freedoms.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Mr Deneen's fixation on the essence of liberalism leads to the second big problem of his book: his failure to recognise liberalism's ability to reform itself and address its internal problems."

The author clearly criticizes Deneen for two main things -> narrow view of liberalism's essence + ignoring liberalism's self-reform ability.

From passage: "He is also right to assert that the world has much to learn from the premodern notions of liberty as self-mastery and self-denial."

Wait -> the author actually agrees with Deneen about premodern notions! This is praise, not criticism.

🔴 Option 1 -> valid criticism -> author directly says Deneen fails to recognize liberalism's historical ability to reform itself, citing late 19th century examples

🔴 Option 2 -> valid criticism -> author disagrees with Deneen's conclusion that we need "liberation from liberalism itself" and suggests liberalism should reform instead ("up your game, or else")

🟢 Option 3 -> NOT a criticism -> author actually supports Deneen's reference to premodern notions, saying "he is right to assert that the world has much to learn from premodern notions"

🔴 Option 4 -> valid criticism -> author faults Deneen's "fixation on the essence of liberalism" and narrow view that liberalism just means "freeing individuals from constraints"

The key insight -> when author says Deneen is "right" about something, that's agreement, not criticism. Option 3 is the only one where author agrees with Deneen rather than criticizing him.

questions.question_text: The author of the passage refers to "the Davos elite" to illustrate his views on:

options.label: A
options.text: the unlikelihood of a return to the liberalism of the past as long as the rich continue to benefit from the decline in liberal values.

options.label: B
options.text: the way the debate around liberalism has been captured by the rich who have managed to insulate themselves from economic hardships.

options.label: C
options.text: the fact that the rise in liberalism had led to a greater interest in shared futures from unlikely social classes.

options.label: D
options.text: the hypocrisy of the liberal rich, who profess to subscribe to liberal values while cornering most of the wealth

questions.explanation_text:
Find where the author mentions "the Davos elite" and what point he's making.

Step 1: Find the Davos reference in the passage. Look for the context around it -> What is the author trying to prove or show?

From passage: "What better proof of this than the vision of 1,000 private planes whisking their occupants to Davos to discuss the question of 'creating a shared future in a fragmented world'?"

Step 2: Understand the author's point -> He just talked about a huge gap between what liberalism claims and reality. The Davos example shows this gap perfectly.

Step 3: Find the second Davos reference for more clarity:

From passage: "The biggest enemy of liberalism is not so much atomisation but old-fashioned greed, as members of the Davos elite pile their plates ever higher with perks and share options."

Step 4: Connect the dots -> Rich people fly private planes to talk about helping everyone + they're greedy and hoard wealth = hypocrisy

Elimination Strategy:

Students often get confused between options 2 and 4 because both talk about the rich. Here's how to tell them apart:

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> talks about "return to past liberalism" but the Davos reference isn't about going backwards, it's about current hypocrisy

🟠 Option 2 -> context-shift -> says they "captured the debate" but passage shows them as hypocrites, not debate-controllers. They're not controlling discussions, they're just being fake.

🔴 Option 3 -> opposite-meaning -> says something positive about "greater interest in shared futures" but the Davos reference is clearly negative and sarcastic

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> captures the exact hypocrisy: they say they care about shared futures but do greedy things like private planes and hoarding wealth

Key insight: The author uses Davos elite to show the contradiction between what liberal rich people say and what they actually do.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements are evidence of the decline of liberalism today, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: "And technological advances are reducing ever more areas of work into meaningless drudgery."

options.label: B
options.text: "'The gap between liberalism's claims about itself and the lived reality of the citizenry' is now so wide that 'the lie can no longer be accepted.'"

options.label: C
options.text: "Democracy has degenerated into a theatre of the absurd."

options.label: D
options.text: "the creation of a business aristocracy, the rise of vast companies"

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which statement is NOT evidence of liberalism's decline today. The key is to check if each quote talks about current problems or something else.

From passage: "Over the past four centuries liberalism has been so successful that it has driven all its opponents off the battlefield. Now it is disintegrating, destroyed by a mix of hubris and internal contradictions"

The passage lists current problems with liberalism -> then mentions some historical context -> we need to separate what's happening now vs. what happened before.

Let us trace where each quote appears:

🟢 Option 1 is correct -> While mentioned, it's not presented as the main evidence of decline the author accepts - the author shifts focus to greed instead

🟠 Option 2 -> Current evidence -> The gap quote is from paragraph 1 describing present-day disillusionment

🟠 Option 3 -> Current evidence -> "Democracy has degenerated into a theatre of the absurd" is from paragraph 1 about current state

🟠 Option 4 -> Historical context -> "creation of a business aristocracy, the rise of vast companies" comes from paragraph 3 describing late 19th century problems, not current ones

questions.question_text: The author of the passage is likely to disagree with all of the following statements, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the essence of liberalism lies in greater individual self-expression and freedoms.

options.label: B
options.text: claims about liberalism's disintegration are exaggerated and misunderstand its core features.

options.label: C
options.text: if we accept that liberalism is a dying ideal, we must work to find a viable substitute.

options.label: D
options.text: liberalism was the dominant ideal in the past century, but it had to reform itself to remain so.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which statement the author would agree with (since it asks which they would disagree with, EXCEPT).

Let us trace the author's main argument about liberalism through the passage.

From passage: "Mr Deneen's fixation on the essence of liberalism leads to the second big problem of his book: his failure to recognise liberalism's ability to reform itself and address its internal problems."

The author's core belief -> liberalism can reform itself instead of dying. The author gives historical examples of how liberalism fixed problems in late 19th century America.

From passage: "Rather than dying, liberalism reformed itself."

So the author thinks liberalism survives by adapting and changing, not by staying the same or dying.

Let's check each option to see what the author would disagree with:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> The author specifically criticizes this narrow view. Deneen says liberalism is just about "freeing individuals from constraints" but author says liberalism has "a wide range of intellectual traditions" that balance rights and responsibilities.

🟠 Option 2 -> author agrees -> claims about disintegration are "exaggerated" - but the author does acknowledge real problems exist ("the record of liberalism in recent years has been dismal")

🔴 Option 3 -> premise-rejection -> The author doesn't accept that liberalism is dying in the first place, so finding a substitute isn't needed. Author believes in reform, not replacement.

🟢 Option 4 -> author agrees -> This perfectly captures the author's main thesis about liberalism's historical success through self-reform.

questions.question_text: Based on the passage, we can infer that the opposite of fast fashion, 'slow fashion', would most likely refer to clothes that:

options.label: A
options.text: do not shed microfibres.

options.label: B
options.text: do not bleed toxins and dyes.

options.label: C
options.text: are sold by genuine vintage stores.

options.label: D
options.text: are of high quality and long lasting.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the passage suggests would be the opposite of fast fashion. Let us trace through the passage to see what solutions it offers.

The passage first explains fast fashion problems -> then explores second-hand shopping as a solution -> but warns about microfiber issues with older clothes -> then gives the key advice for what actually works.

From passage: "They would be well advised to buy high-quality items that shed less and last longer as this combats both microfibre pollution and excess garments ending up in landfills."

This sentence is the key - it directly tells us what the passage thinks is the real solution to fast fashion's problems.

The thought process: Fast fashion = cheap, disposable, wasteful -> So slow fashion = opposite = high quality, durable, long-lasting

🟠 Option 1 -> overstates -> says clothes "do not shed" microfibres, but passage only says high-quality items shed "less," not zero

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions one problem (toxins/dyes) but misses the main solution the passage focuses on (durability and quality)

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> passage mentions vintage stores but doesn't say being sold by them defines what makes clothes better - focuses on the quality of items, not where they're sold

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> directly matches the passage's advice: "high-quality items that... last longer" - captures both the quality and durability aspects the passage emphasizes

The passage clearly states that buying high-quality, long-lasting items is the solution to fast fashion's environmental problems.

questions.question_text: The act of "thrifting", as described in the passage, can be considered ironic because it:

options.label: A
options.text: offers luxury clothing at cut-rate prices.

options.label: B
options.text: is not cost-effective for retailers.

options.label: C
options.text: is an anti-consumerist attitude.

options.label: D
options.text: has created environmental problems.

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace through the passage to find this contradiction.

From passage: "So you're cool and you care about the planet; you've killed two birds with one stone. But do people simply purchase a second-hand item, flash it on Instagram with #vintage and call it a day without considering whether what they are doing is actually effective?"

The passage sets up thrifting as seeming environmentally good -> but then reveals a hidden problem. The irony comes from the Patagonia study showing old clothes actually cause different environmental damage.

From passage: "According to a study commissioned by Patagonia, for instance, older clothes shed more microfibres. These can end up in our rivers and seas after just one wash due to the worn material, thus contributing to microfibre pollution."

Thought process: People think thrifting helps environment -> but worn clothes shed microfibers -> microfibers pollute oceans -> so "eco-friendly" thrifting actually harms environment differently

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> mentions pricing but irony is about environmental impact, not economics

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> talks about retailer costs, but passage focuses on consumer behavior and environmental effects

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> passage doesn't frame thrifting as anti-consumerist movement, misses the environmental irony completely

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> captures the core irony perfectly: activity meant to help environment actually creates environmental problems through microfiber pollution

questions.question_text: The central idea of the passage would be undermined if

options.label: A
options.text: second-hand stores sold only high-quality clothes.

options.label: B
options.text: clothes were not thrown and burnt in landfills

options.label: C
options.text: Primark and Boohoo recycled their clothes for vintage stores.

options.label: D
options.text: customers bought all their clothes online.

questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Identify the central idea -> The passage argues that second-hand shopping is a good alternative to fast fashion for everyone to help save the planet.

Step 2: Look for what would weaken this solution -> Something that makes second-hand shopping less effective or accessible.

From passage: "If everyone bought just one used item in a year, it would save 449 million lbs of waste, equivalent to the weight of 1 million Polar bears."

The key insight -> The passage wants mass participation in second-hand shopping. The solution works best when many people can access it, not just wealthy buyers.

Let's eliminate the wrong options:

🟢 Option 2 -> supports the main idea -> If clothes weren't thrown in landfills, that would actually help the environment. This supports the passage's goals.

🟢 Option 3 -> supports the main idea -> If Primark and Boohoo recycled clothes, that would reduce waste. This also helps the environmental cause.

🟠 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> Online shopping doesn't contradict second-hand shopping. People can still buy second-hand clothes online.

🔴 Option 1 -> undermines access -> If stores only sold high-quality clothes, they'd be too expensive for most people. This would limit who can participate in second-hand shopping.

From passage: "Brits buy more garments than any other country in Europe" and the passage promotes second-hand as alternative to "Primark and Boohoo"

The logic -> Primark and Boohoo customers shop there because it's cheap -> If second-hand stores only sold expensive, high-quality items -> These customers couldn't afford them -> They'd stick with fast fashion -> The environmental solution fails.

The passage needs second-hand shopping to be accessible to everyone, not just people who can afford luxury items.

questions.question_text: According to the author, companies like ThredUP have not caught on in the UK for all of the following reasons EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: luxury brands want to maintain their brand image.

options.label: B
options.text: the British don't buy second-hand clothing.

options.label: C
options.text: recycling is currently not financially attractive for luxury brands.

options.label: D
options.text: luxury brands do not like their product to be devalued.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Luxury brands would rather not circulate their latest season stock around the globe to be sold at a cheaper price, which is why companies like ThredUP, a US fashion resale marketplace, have not yet caught on in the UK. There will always be a market for consignment but there is also a whole generation of people who have been taught that only buying new products is the norm; second-hand luxury goods are not in their psyche... high-end retailers would rather put brand before sustainability."

Thought process: Author gives specific reasons -> luxury brands avoid cheaper resale -> generation taught to buy new only -> brands prioritize image over sustainability -> recycling not cost-effective yet

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> brand image concern is mentioned but this reason IS given in passage

🟢 Option 2 -> correct answer -> passage says "there will always be a market for consignment" and mentions London's many vintage shops -> doesn't say British don't buy second-hand clothing at all

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> recycling cost-effectiveness is mentioned as a barrier -> this reason IS given

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> devaluation concern is mentioned when talking about cheaper prices -> this reason IS given

Key insight: The passage actually supports that British do buy second-hand clothing -> mentions vintage shop trend and consignment market -> just says luxury second-hand specifically isn't in people's "psyche" yet

questions.question_text: The author sees the rise of Netflix in Europe as:

options.label: A
options.text: a looming cultural threat.

options.label: B
options.text: a unifying force.

options.label: C
options.text: filling an entertainment gap.

options.label: D
options.text: an economic threat.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the author's personal view on Netflix's rise in Europe, not what politicians think about it.

Step-by-step process:

  1. Identify who has what opinion -> politicians vs. author
  2. Focus on final paragraph -> author's conclusion
  3. Look for tone indicators -> "should not be" + "irony" shows author disagrees with politicians

From passage: "They should not be. An irony of European integration is that it is often American companies that facilitate it... Now Netflix and friends pump the same content into homes across a continent, making culture a cross-border endeavour, too."

Thought process:

Author starts with politicians' fears -> then says "They should not be" worried -> explains Netflix actually helps European unity -> gives examples of shared experiences like "bingeing on the same series" -> compares to sharing currency and vaccines

The key insight: Author thinks politicians are wrong to worry. Netflix actually brings Europeans together through shared cultural experiences.

🔴 Option 1 -> context-shift -> this is what politicians think ("cultural sovereignty" concerns), not the author's view. Author clearly disagrees with this fear.

🟢 Option 2 is correct -> perfectly captures author's view that Netflix creates shared experiences across Europe, just like shared currency or vaccines do for unity.

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> too narrow focus. Author isn't talking about entertainment gaps but about cultural unity and integration.

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> passage discusses cultural concerns, not economic threats. Author focuses on cultural integration benefits.

Key elimination tip: When passage shows multiple viewpoints, always check whose opinion the question asks for. Here, politicians fear Netflix but author celebrates it as unifying force.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following research findings would weaken the author's conclusion in the final paragraph?

options.label: A
options.text: Research shows there is a wide variance in the popularity and viewing of Netflix shows across different EU countries.

options.label: B
options.text: Research shows that Netflix has been gradually losing market share to other streaming television service providers.

options.label: C
options.text: Research shows that Netflix hits produced in France are very popular with North American audiences.

options.label: D
options.text: Research shows that older women across the EU enjoy watching romantic comedies on Netflix, whereas younger women prefer historical fiction dramas.

questions.explanation_text:
" This supports European integration because Europeans need "something in common."

From passage: "Now Netflix and friends pump the same content into homes across a continent, making culture a cross-border endeavour, too. If Europeans are to share a currency, bail each other out in times of financial need and share vaccines in a pandemic, then they need to have something in common—even if it is just bingeing on the same series."

Author's logic: Netflix delivers same content everywhere -> Europeans watch same shows -> shared culture -> supports integration

To weaken this, we need evidence that Netflix doesn't create shared experiences across Europe.

🟢 Option 1 is correct -> directly contradicts the shared culture claim -> If Netflix shows have "wide variance in popularity" across EU countries, then people aren't actually sharing the same cultural experiences. Different countries watching different things = no shared culture.

🔴 Option 2 -> scope-error -> This is about Netflix's business performance vs competitors, not about whether Netflix creates shared cultural experiences when people do watch it.

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> French shows being popular in North America doesn't affect whether Europeans share cultural experiences with each other through Netflix.

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> Shows different demographics like different genres, but this is still within the same cultural ecosystem. Age preferences don't break the cross-border sharing concept - older women across all EU countries still share romantic comedies.

The key confusion students face: Options 2 and 4 seem relevant to Netflix. But Option 2 is about market competition, and Option 4 actually supports shared culture (same age groups across borders like same genres). Only Option 1 directly attacks the "shared experience" foundation of the author's argument.

questions.question_text: Based on information provided in the passage, all of the following are true, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: European television productions have the potential to become global hits.

options.label: B
options.text: national broadcasters dominate in the EU in terms of total television viewing hours.

options.label: C
options.text: only half of Netflix's original programming in the EU is now produced in America.

options.label: D
options.text: Netflix has been able to transform itself into a truly European entity.

questions.explanation_text:
Need to check each option against passage evidence carefully.

From passage: "Now Netflix has offices across Europe. But ultimately the big decisions rest with American executives."

Step-by-step approach -> Read each option -> Find supporting evidence in passage -> The one WITHOUT clear support is our answer.

Many students get confused between options 3 and 4 because both mention Netflix's changes. Here's how to think through it:

Option 1 -> European shows can become global hits

  • Passage clearly shows "Lupin" (French show) became global hit
  • Easy elimination -> This is TRUE

Option 2 -> National broadcasters dominate viewing hours

  • Passage says "national broadcasters still dominate"
  • Streaming services only account for "about a third" of viewing
  • Easy elimination -> This is TRUE

Option 3 -> Only half of Netflix's content is now American

  • Passage states: "In 2015, about 75% was American; now the figure is half"
  • This is TRUE

🟢 Option 4 -> scope-error -> claims complete transformation but passage shows mixed reality

  • Yes, Netflix has European offices BUT "ultimately big decisions rest with American executives"
  • Content still seems "stuck in mid-Atlantic uncanny valley"
  • This overstates Netflix's European transformation -> This is FALSE

From passage: "But ultimately the big decisions rest with American executives. This makes European politicians nervous."

The key insight: Having local offices ≠ becoming truly European entity when core control remains American.

questions.question_text: Based only on information provided in the passage, which one of the following hypothetical Netflix shows would be most successful with audiences across the EU?

options.label: A
options.text: An Italian comedy show hosted by an international star.

options.label: B
options.text: An original German TV science fiction production.

options.label: C
options.text: A murder mystery drama set in North Africa and France.

options.label: D
options.text: A trans-Atlantic romantic drama set in Europe and America.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Not everything works across borders. Comedy sometimes struggles. Whodunits and bloodthirsty maelstroms between arch Romans and uppity tribesmen have a more universal appeal."

The key insight is that the passage tells us directly which genres succeed internationally and which struggle. We need to match the options against these success patterns.

The passage also shows us a real example: From passage: "shows such as 'Lupin', a French crime caper on Netflix, can become global hits"

So our thought process: What genres work across borders? -> Murder mysteries and crime stories do well -> Comedy struggles -> Look for the option that matches successful patterns

🔴 Option 1 -> directly contradicts passage -> "Comedy sometimes struggles" across borders, so an Italian comedy would face this exact problem

🟠 Option 2 -> context-shift -> Passage says "German television is not always built for export" and doesn't mention science fiction as having universal appeal

🟢 Option 3 is correct -> matches successful patterns exactly -> "Whodunits have universal appeal" + "Lupin" (crime story) became a "global hit"

🟠 Option 4 -> negative association -> Passage warns Netflix content can get "stuck in an uncanny valley somewhere in the mid-Atlantic" which sounds like this exact type of show

The passage gives us a simple formula: Crime/mystery stories = universal success, Comedy = struggles across borders. Option 3 fits the winning formula perfectly.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: ___ (1) ___ At the core of development economics lies the idea of 'productive dualism': that poor countries' economies are split between a narrow 'modern' sector that uses advanced technologies and a larger 'traditional' sector characterized by very low productivity ___ (2) ___ . While this distinction between developing and advanced economies may have made some sense in the 1950s and 1960s, it no longer appears to be very relevant. A combination of forces have produced a widening gap between the winners and those left behind ___ (3) ___ . Convergence between poor and rich parts of the economy was arrested and regional disparities widened ___ (4) ___ . As a result, policymakers in advanced economies are now grappling with the same questions that have long pre-occupied developing economies: mainly how to close the gap with the more advanced parts of the economy.

Sentence: Dualism was long held as the defining feature of developing countries in contrast to developed countries, where frontier technologies and high productivity were assumed to prevail.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
Step-by-step approach: Find where the missing sentence fits best by understanding what it adds to the paragraph flow.

From passage: "At the core of development economics lies the idea of 'productive dualism': that poor countries' economies are split between a narrow 'modern' sector that uses advanced technologies and a larger 'traditional' sector characterized by very low productivity"

Thought process: The missing sentence talks about dualism as a defining feature of developing vs developed countries -> This needs to come right after dualism is introduced -> Then the passage can explain why this view is outdated -> Perfect logical flow.

Option elimination strategy:

🔴 Option 1 -> placement-error -> Puts definition before concept introduction. Like defining "photosynthesis" before saying "plants make food" - backwards logic.

🟢 Option 2 -> perfect-fit -> Sentence 1 introduces dualism -> Missing sentence explains traditional view of dualism -> Sentence 2 says this view is outdated. Clean logical bridge.

🟠 Option 3 -> timing-error -> Comes after saying dualism is "no longer relevant" - why explain the old view after dismissing it? Like describing horse carriages after saying cars replaced them.

🟠 Option 4 -> context-shift -> Talks about traditional economic theory when paragraph is ending with current policy challenges - completely different focus.

Key insight: The missing sentence is a bridge that explains the traditional view right after the concept is introduced, setting up why that view became outdated.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: Research has hypothesised that the earliest evidence of human lip kissing originated in a very specific geographical location in South Asia 3,500 years ago ___ (1) ___ . From there it may have spread to other regions, simultaneously accelerating the spread of the herpes simplex virus 1. According to Dr Troels Pank Arbøll and Dr Sophie Lund Rasmussen, who in a new article in the journal Science draw on a range of written sources from the earliest Mesopotamian societies, kissing was already a well-established practice 4,500 years ago in the Middle East ___ (2) ___ . In ancient Mesopotamia, people wrote in cuneiform script on clay tablets ___ (3) ___ . Many thousands of these clay tablets have survived to this day, and they contain clear examples that kissing was considered a part of romantic intimacy in ancient times ___ (4) ___ . "Kissing could also have been part of friendships and family members' relations," says Dr Troels Pank Arbøll, an expert on the history of medicine in Mesopotamia.

Sentence: And probably much earlier, moving the documentation for kissing back 1,000 years compared to what was acknowledged in the scientific community.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
The paragraph mentions two time periods: South Asia at 3,500 years ago (mentioned first) and Middle East at 4,500 years ago (mentioned second). Notice that 4,500 years is actually OLDER (earlier in history) than 3,500 years! The difference is exactly 1,000 years.

Missing sentence says

The sentence says "And probably much earlier, moving the documentation for kissing back 1,000 years..." This means we found evidence that's 1,000 years OLDER than what was previously thought.

Option 2 is correct as: The missing sentence should come right after the Middle East evidence is presented. This makes perfect sense because the paragraph just told us about NEW evidence from the Middle East (4,500 years ago), and the missing sentence immediately clarifies that this moves the timeline back 1,000 years from the South Asia evidence (3,500 years). The math checks out: 4,500 minus 3,500 equals 1,000 years earlier. It connects the two pieces of evidence smoothly.

Eliminating other options:

Option 1: This position is too early. We haven't mentioned the Middle East evidence yet. If we put the sentence here, readers would be confused about what "1,000 years earlier" refers to.

Option 3: This section talks about clay tablets and writing methods, not about comparing timelines. The missing sentence is about timeline revision, so it doesn't fit here.

Option 4: This section talks about romantic intimacy examples, not about when kissing started. The missing sentence discusses historical dating, so it's completely out of place here.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. The banning of Northern Lights could be considered a precursor to censoring books for "moral", world view or religious reasons.
  2. Attempts to ban books are attempts to silence authors who have summoned immense courage in telling their stories.
  3. Now the banning and challenging of books in the US has escalated to an unprecedented level.
  4. The widely acclaimed fantasy novel Northern Lights was banned in some parts of the US, and was the second most challenged book in the US.
  5. The American Library Association documented an unparalleled number of reported book challenges in 2022, about 2,500 unique titles.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Look for a logical flow between sentences. Most coherent paragraphs follow a pattern -> specific example -> broader trend -> supporting data.

Step 2: Group sentences by similar themes:

  • Sentences 3, 4, 5 all talk about specific facts and data about book banning
  • Sentences 1 and 4 both mention "Northern Lights"
  • Sentence 2 talks about the philosophy behind book banning

From passage: "The widely acclaimed fantasy novel Northern Lights was banned in some parts of the US" and "The banning of Northern Lights could be considered a precursor to censoring books"

The logical flow works like this: Specific example (Northern Lights banned) -> This as precursor to broader trend -> Current escalation -> Data supporting this escalation.

Elimination Process:

🟢 Sentences 4, 1, 3, 5 form coherent flow:

  • Start with specific example (Northern Lights)
  • Connect to broader implications (precursor to wider censorship)
  • Show current escalation
  • Provide supporting data (2022 statistics)

🔴 Sentence 2 -> context-shift: While related to book banning, it shifts from factual reporting to philosophical commentary about authors' courage. It doesn't fit the data-driven narrative that the other four sentences create together.

Answer: 2

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Self-care particularly links to loneliness, behavioural problems, and negative academic outcomes.

2."Latchkey children" refers to children who routinely return home from school to empty homes and take care of themselves for extended periods of time.

  1. Although self-care generally points to negative outcomes, it is important to consider that the bulk of research has yet to track long-term consequences.
  2. In research and practice, the phrase "children in self-care" has come to replace latchkey in an effort to more accurately reflect the nature of their circumstances.
  3. Although parents might believe self-care would be beneficial for development, recent research has found quite the opposite.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: Let us trace the logical connection -> Sentence 2 defines "latchkey children" -> Sentence 4 shows how terminology changed -> Sentence 1 lists negative outcomes -> Sentence 5 contrasts parent beliefs with research findings.

The thought process: Find the main story first -> Look for the sentence that doesn't belong in that story.

The main story here is about children in self-care and their negative outcomes. Sentences 2, 4, 1, and 5 create a clear narrative about this topic.

Why sentence 3 is the odd one out:

Sentences 2-4-1-5 flow like this:

  • Definition of latchkey children
  • How the term evolved to "children in self-care"
  • Specific negative outcomes found
  • How research contradicts parent beliefs

Sentence 3 suddenly introduces doubt about the research by saying "bulk of research has yet to track long-term consequences." This contradicts the definitive tone of the other sentences that present clear findings about negative outcomes.

The other 4 sentences present established facts and findings, while sentence 3 questions the completeness of those findings. It breaks the flow of presenting concrete information about self-care's negative impacts.

Correct Answer: 3

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Like the ants that make up a colony, no single neuron holds complex information like self-awareness, hope or pride.
  2. Although the human brain is not yet understood enough to identify the mechanism by which emergence functions, most neurobiologists agree that complex interconnections among the parts give rise to qualities that belong only to the whole.
  3. Nonetheless, the sum of all neurons in the nervous system generate complex human emotions like fear and joy, none of which can be attributed to a single neuron.
  4. Human consciousness is often called an emergent property of the human brain.
questions.explanation_text:
Step-by-Step Process:

First, scan for the topic sentence -> Sentence 4 introduces "emergent property" - this is our main concept, so it should come first.

Next, look for connecting words and logical flow:

  • Sentence 1 has "Like the ants" -> gives analogy to explain emergence
  • Sentence 3 starts with "Nonetheless" -> shows contrast, needs something before it
  • Sentence 2 has "Although" -> can work anywhere but flows better as conclusion

From passage: "Human consciousness is often called an emergent property of the human brain" (Sentence 4) introduces the main idea.

Logical flow: Introduction -> Analogy -> Contrast/Extension -> Expert conclusion

Elimination Process:

🟢 4132 is correct -> Natural flow: concept introduction -> analogy -> extension with "nonetheless" -> scientific backing

The key is recognizing:

  • Sentence 4 = topic sentence (introduces main concept)
  • Sentence 1 = analogy (explains the concept using ants)
  • Sentence 3 = extension ("Nonetheless" continues the thought)
  • Sentence 2 = conclusion (expert opinion wraps up discussion)

Quick tip: In para jumbles, look for transition words like "nonetheless," "although," "like" -> they show you how sentences connect!

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Contemporary African writing like 'The Bottled Leopard' voices this theme using two children and two backgrounds to juxtapose two varying cultures.
  2. Chukwuemeka Ike explores the conflict, and casts the Western tradition as condescending, enveloping and unaccommodating towards local African practice.
  3. However, their views contradict the reality, for a rich and sustaining local cultural ethos exists for all who care, to see and experience.
  4. Western Christian concepts tend to deny or feign ignorance about the existence of a genuine and enduring indigenous African tradition.
questions.explanation_text:
To solve paragraph jumbling, find the opening sentence that introduces the main topic, then follow the logical flow of ideas.

Step 1: Look for the sentence that introduces the main theme without referring to anything else.

Step 2: Find sentences with connecting words like "however," "this theme," etc. that link back to previous ideas.

Step 3: Check if examples come after general statements.

From passage: "Western Christian concepts tend to deny or feign ignorance about the existence of a genuine and enduring indigenous African tradition."

This sentence introduces the main conflict → no prior reference needed → perfect opening sentence.

From passage: "However, their views contradict the reality, for a rich and sustaining local cultural ethos exists for all who care, to see and experience."

"However" + "their views" → clearly responds to sentence 4's Western views → comes right after 4.

From passage: "Contemporary African writing like 'The Bottled Leopard' voices this theme using two children and two backgrounds to juxtapose two varying cultures."

"This theme" → refers back to the conflict discussed earlier → needs context first → comes after the conflict is established.

Elimination Process:

🟢 Sequence 4312 → correct flow → Problem (4) → Counter-argument (3) → Literary example (1) → Specific author details (2)

Any sequence not starting with 4 → scope-error → other sentences need prior context to make sense

Any sequence putting sentence 1 before establishing the conflict → context-shift → "this theme" would have no reference point

Any sequence separating 4 and 3 → logical-break → "However, their views" in sentence 3 directly responds to sentence 4's Western views

The answer flows: Western denial (4) → African reality exists (3) → Literature shows this conflict (1) → Specific example of author's approach (2)

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Heat waves are becoming longer, frequent and intense due to climate change. The impacts of extreme heat are unevenly experienced; with older people and young children, those with pre-existing medical conditions and on low incomes significantly more vulnerable. Adaptation to heatwaves is a significant public policy concern. Research conducted among at-risk people in the UK reveals that even vulnerable people do not perceive themselves as at risk of extreme heat; therefore, early warnings of extreme heat events do not perform as intended. This suggests that understanding how extreme heat is narrated is very important. The news media play a central role in this process and can help warn people about the potential danger, as well as about impacts on infrastructure and society.

options.label: A
options.text: Heatwaves pose an enormous risk; the media plays a pivotal role in alerting people to this danger.

options.label: B
options.text: Protection from heat waves is important but current reports and public policies seem ineffective.

options.label: C
options.text: People are vulnerable to heatwaves caused due to climate change, measures taken are ineffective.

options.label: D
options.text: News stories help in warning about heatwaves, but they have to become more effective.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the option that best captures the main themes and scope of what's being discussed.

From passage: "Heat waves are becoming longer, frequent and intense due to climate change" and "The news media play a central role in this process and can help warn people about the potential danger"

The passage covers two big ideas: heatwaves are a serious and growing threat -> media has an important role in dealing with this threat. The research finding about people not seeing themselves as at risk is supporting detail for why media's role matters.

Option Analysis:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures both main themes: serious risk from heatwaves + media's pivotal role in alerting people

🟠 Option 2 -> scope-error -> focuses too much on policy ineffectiveness, misses the central role of media that the passage emphasizes

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> mentions vulnerability and ineffective measures correctly but completely ignores media's role, which is a key theme

🔴 Option 4 -> too-narrow -> only talks about news stories becoming more effective, misses the broader picture about heatwave risks and vulnerable populations

The passage talks about two main things equally: the serious threat from heatwaves AND media's important role. Option 1 is the only one that captures both themes without getting stuck on just the supporting details about perception problems or policy issues.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

People spontaneously create counterfactual alternatives to reality when they think "if only" or "what if" and imagine how the past could have been different. The mind computes counterfactuals for many reasons. Counterfactuals explain the past and prepare for the future, they implicate various relations including causal ones, and they affect intentions and decisions. They modulate emotions such as regret and relief, and they support moral judgments such as blame. The ability to create counterfactuals develops throughout childhood and contributes to reasoning about other people's beliefs, including their false beliefs.

options.label: A
options.text: People create counterfactual alternatives to reality for various reasons, including reasoning about other people's beliefs.

options.label: B
options.text: Counterfactual thinking helps to reverse past and future actions and reason out false beliefs.

options.label: C
options.text: Counterfactual alternatives to reality are created for a variety of reasons and is part of one's developmental process.

options.label: D
options.text: Counterfactuals help people to prepare for the future by understanding intentions and making decisions.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the option that best captures the essence - meaning it should cover the main ideas without missing key points or going off track.

The passage has two big ideas:

  1. People create counterfactuals for many different reasons (explains past, prepares future, affects emotions, supports judgments, etc.)
  2. This ability develops during childhood

From passage: "The mind computes counterfactuals for many reasons" and "The ability to create counterfactuals develops throughout childhood"

My thought process -> Look for option that mentions both the variety of reasons AND the developmental aspect -> This will be the most complete summary

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> mentions "various reasons" correctly but only highlights one specific reason (reasoning about beliefs) when passage lists many important functions like emotions, decisions, moral judgments

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> says counterfactuals "reverse past and future actions" but passage says they "explain past and prepare for future" - completely different meaning and misunderstands what counterfactuals actually do

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> focuses only on future preparation aspect but ignores all other functions mentioned (emotions, moral judgments, explaining past) and misses developmental component entirely

🟢 Option 3 is correct -> captures both key elements: "variety of reasons" (matches passage's "many reasons") AND "developmental process" (matches "develops throughout childhood") - most complete summary without missing main points
